name: Rafael Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two five-axis machining centres at a company that makes metal parts for aircraft, mostly titanium brackets and housings. Five-axis means the cutting tool can come at the part from almost any angle, so you can make really complicated shapes in one go. I load the blanks, set up the tools, run the programs, measure the first part on the inspection machine and adjust. I love the precision, a bracket for a plane has to be right to a hundredth of a millimetre. What wears me out is the paperwork, every part has to be traced.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use software or AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, every day. I use AI to help me tidy up the cutting programs and to work out faster tool paths, and then I check everything twice, because it's aircraft parts. On weekends I do a bit of programming for two small machine shops in town who can't afford a full-time programmer. My dream is to have my own shop one day, something I can build up and maybe pass on to my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a good tool and I'll keep using it. I'd tell people at work that it's not going to replace them, so they might as well learn it. Online I'd probably post a few tips about AI for machining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd actually be good for me. I'd be one of the few operators who uses it properly, so I'd stay ahead. If AI stays this size, it's a sharp new tool in my box, and most of the lads at work haven't even opened the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at work, keep the weekend programming, and keep saving for my own shop. I've got a flat I rent out and about a year of savings, so in two or three years I'd buy my first second-hand machine. Clara and I would get married next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited about the shop, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Clara.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's an accountant, she's the one who makes my shop plans actually add up. We met at church, at a summer festival, five years ago. She's cautious where I'm not, which is probably good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your shop make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small batches of precision parts, for medical and maybe aerospace once I've got the certificates. The big firms don't want small jobs, and that's where a good small shop can make money.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool and I'll keep using it. I'd tell colleagues it won't replace them, so they might as well learn it, and post a few machining tips online.
S0.think: Honestly, it'd be good for me, because I'm one of the few operators who uses AI properly. I'd stay ahead of the rest.
S0.do: Keeps working, keeps his weekend programming jobs and saves toward his own shop, aiming to buy a first second-hand machine within two or three years. Marries Clara next year.
S0.feel: Calm and excited about the shop.
S0.quote: If AI stays this size, it's a sharp new tool in my box, and most of the lads at work haven't even opened the box.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is ambitious and entrepreneurial, with weekend programming work and a clear plan for his own shop. His traditional side shows in wanting something to pass on to his children. His fiancée balances his appetite for risk with caution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people who are willing to learn. Companies should be free to adapt, and workers should step up rather than wait to be rescued. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is my moment. Small shops that use AI and robots well could compete with big ones. Steady change is exactly what a man with one machine and a good laptop needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the shop plan. In the first year I'd buy a second-hand machining centre and a small robot arm to load it, set it up in a rented unit and run it evenings and weekends. I'd keep my day job until the shop covered my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't running a shop on evenings and weekends wear you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or two, yes. Clara says I'd see more of the robot arm than of her. But that's what building something takes, my grandfather did the same with his carpentry shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Manuel, who's fifty and still does setups by feel. He's good, but he won't touch the AI tools. If he'd let me, I'd show him, but he thinks I'm a show-off.

S1.say: I'd say steady change is an opportunity for people willing to learn. Companies should be free to adapt, workers should step up, and apprenticeships matter more than ever.
S1.think: This is my moment, because small shops that use AI and robots well could compete with the big ones. Steady change suits a man with one machine and a good laptop.
S1.do: Speeds up his shop plan, buying a second-hand machining centre and a small robot arm in the first year and running it from a rented unit on evenings and weekends. Keeps his day job until the shop covers his wage.
S1.quote: Steady change is exactly what a man with one machine and a good laptop needs.
S1.fieldNote: Rafael sees steady disruption as a chance to build his business rather than a threat. He links his ambition to his grandfather's carpentry shop. He'd help an older colleague if allowed, though there's some friction there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than anyone can handle, and the government shouldn't make it worse with clumsy rules. I'd say people should rely on their families and their own work as much as possible. But I'd admit it's going to be tough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one worries me. Two years isn't enough time to build a shop, and if AI can run machines, programme them and inspect parts, then the big firms with robots and money win. My little shop would be finished before it started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and put some money into the companies building the robots, because if you can't beat them, own a piece. I'd still buy one machine and a robot arm, because owning a little is better than nothing. And I'd lean on Clara's planning and my family's advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. For the first time, my plan feels too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still buy a machine with only two years' warning. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man who owns a machine has something to bargain with, and a man who just runs one doesn't. It might lose value, but I'd rather be on the owning side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your colleagues in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To save, and to stop waiting for the government to fix it. I know that sounds hard, but I think families and communities will do more for them than any office in the capital.

S2.say: I'd say it's moving faster than anyone can handle, and the government shouldn't make it worse with clumsy rules. People should rely on family and their own work, though it will be tough.
S2.think: This one worries me, because two years isn't enough to build a shop. The big firms with robots and money would win before my little shop even got going.
S2.do: Saves harder and invests in robotics companies, while still buying one machine and a robot arm to be on the owning side. Leans on Clara's planning and his family.
S2.feel: Anxious, feeling for the first time that his plan is too slow.
S2.quote: a man who owns a machine has something to bargain with, and a man who just runs one doesn't.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens Rafael's dream of building a shop more than his current job. His answer is ownership, even a small amount. He keeps his free-market line in public while privately expecting big firms to win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who are willing to work hard to build something. I'd say the government should stay out of the way and support apprenticeships and small business. And I'd tell young people to get their hands on the machines now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to get the shop going, but it'd be a race against the big firms. I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe a baby. It's tight, but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy the machine and robot arm, rent a unit and start taking jobs from local firms. By year two I'd quit my job and go full time. I'd automate as much of the shop as I could, so it can run at night with no one there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited, but I'd be watching the big firms every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get customers who trust me. In aerospace you don't win a contract with a price, you win it with years of parts that were never wrong. Two years isn't long enough for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One or two, maybe young people as apprentices, like my grandfather took on boys from the village. I'd want the shop to be a place that teaches, not just a box of robots.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for hard workers to build something, and the government should stay out of the way while supporting apprenticeships and small business.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get the shop going, but it'd be a race against the big firms. I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe with a baby, so it's tight but doable.
S3.do: Buys a machine and robot arm in the first year, rents a unit and takes local jobs, then quits his job by year two to go full time. Automates the shop so it can run overnight.
S3.feel: Uneasy but excited, keeping a constant eye on the big firms.
S3.quote: In aerospace you don't win a contract with a price, you win it with years of parts that were never wrong.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Rafael is ready to quit his job and run an automated shop, but sees it as a race. He wants apprentices, linking his business to his grandfather's tradition. Trust built over years is what he thinks wins customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to prepare, and that families and small businesses are the backbone of what comes next. I'd say young people should learn trades and how to use these tools. And I'd say government should keep taxes low for small shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me feel good. I'd have time to build the shop properly, get the aerospace certificates and have a family. I'd be thirty-seven, with a business that runs itself most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd buy the machines and start part time. By year three or four I'd go full time and take on an apprentice. I'd keep investing in the shop and in robotics shares, and use AI for everything from quoting to programming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. More than calm, this is the one I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When AGI arrives, couldn't it run a shop like yours without you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But by then I'd own it, and I'd have customers who know me. If the robots end up doing the work, I want my name on the door of the building they work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My kids, if we have them. I'd want them to learn to work with their hands and their heads, even if machines can do it. Work is how you become a person, and I don't want them to miss that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, and families and small businesses are the backbone of what comes next. Young people should learn trades and tools, and taxes should stay low for small shops.
S4.think: Ten years makes me feel good. I'd have time to build the shop, get the aerospace certificates and have a family, with a business that runs itself most nights by thirty-seven.
S4.do: Buys machines and starts part time in the first two years, then goes full time by year three or four and takes on an apprentice. Keeps investing in the shop and robotics shares and uses AI for quoting and programming.
S4.feel: Calm, even pleased, since this is the picture he'd choose.
S4.quote: If the robots end up doing the work, I want my name on the door of the building they work in.
S4.fieldNote: Rafael is at his most confident with ten years, aiming to own an automated shop with his name on the door. His worry turns to whether his future children will learn the value of work. His traditional values and his appetite for technology sit together without much tension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would kill the shop before it was born. I don't need anyone to save my job, I need enough time to build my own. What would help is easier loans for small shops to buy machines, and fewer rules that only big firms can afford to follow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. For people like me, owning something you built matters more than the money. If the robots take that chance away, that's the real loss.

headlineQuote: I don't need anyone to save my job, I need enough time to build my own.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old five-axis CNC operator at an aerospace parts supplier who uses AI every day, programs machines for small shops on weekends and dreams of his own precision shop. He owns a rental flat, has about a year of savings and is engaged to Clara, an accountant he met at church. He sees steady change as his moment and is calm with ten years' warning, but fast AGI makes him anxious because it would kill his shop before it began. Across every picture his answer is ownership, automation and apprentices, carrying on his grandfather's tradition of building something to pass on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because it would end his plan for his own shop before it could begin.
whatWouldHelp: Easier loans for small shops to buy machines, and fewer rules that only big firms can afford to follow.
